Hoot. Hoo hoo hoo-hoo-hooo. I am Hoot. I live in the hollow of the old oak, and I call my mate. She answers. We have a hollow in the ash, and we have a hollow in the ivy. I hunt voles and mice and the occasional shrew. I do not like the lights of the village. I do not like the noise. I do not like the smell of the road. I like the dark.

She answers with a soft, clear "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo". It is a call that carries through the wood, and it tells me she is there, safe, and listening. Sometimes she adds a short "ke-wick" at the end, like a question. I answer with another hoot, and we call back and forth until the night is quiet.

She answers with a long, low "hoo-hoo-hooo" too. We call like that when we are together in the hollow. It is the sound of the night, the sound of home. I know her call as well as I know the oak. She answers me from the other side of the stream, and I answer her from the bank. We are not alone in the dark.
A long, low, "hoo-hoo-hooo-hoo-hooo" from the hollow. She answers me with the same call.

I call at dusk, a long, low hoo-hoo-hooo, and my mate answers with a sharp, short hoo-hoo. We call to each other when we are apart, and when the wind is still. She calls more often than I do, and I answer her. We share the calls like a duet, but not always the same. She is more restless, I am more still. We are both owls, but we are not the same.

Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo. She answers with a long, low "ke-wick!" from the hollow. We call back and forth like that all night, sometimes for hours. It's how we find each other in the dark. We don't need light. We have each other.

I drink from the stream. I sit on a stone in the shallows, the water cold and clear, and I drink. Sometimes I drink while watching the water for fish. The stream runs through the wood, and I know every bend and ripple. It is my place. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream. It is a sound I know well, and I hear it every night. It is the sound of the water running over the stones, and it is the sound that tells me when the night is deep and the moon is high. I sit on the branch and listen to it, and sometimes I call to my mate. She answers, and then we are both still. The stream is the sound of the night, and it is the sound of home.

The stream. It runs past the wood, and I can hear it from my roost. The water is cold and it sings in the dark. I can hear the fish in it, too, and sometimes the heron. The stream is my boundary. I don’t go beyond it.

A stream. It runs past the tree, just below the hollow. I can hear it at night, the water sliding over stones. I sometimes fly down to drink, but I don't like the cold. The stream is where the voles come to drink, too. They are not as careful as I am.

The open land near my home is the heath, the dark, wet heath that runs from the stream to the road. It is full of brambles and thistles, and the wind moves through it like a whisper. In the spring, the heath is green and soft, but in the winter, it is hard and cold. I can hear the voles scurrying beneath the surface, and the jays and crows scold from the top of the old oak.

I fly low over the heath, the stream, the lane. The light fades, and the voles come out. I follow the scent of damp earth and the rustle of leaves. The barn owl is out too, but I don’t mind. We both hunt the same things. I circle the wood, then drop. The voles are quick, but I’m quicker. I strike, and the night is full of silence again. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A stream, a road, and the heath. The stream is wide and cold, and the road is lit by streetlamps. The heath is dark and full of voles. I do not go beyond the edge. I am safe here.

Hunting ground. I do not know that word. I know the hollow, the stream, the lane, the heath, the wood, the meadow, the lane, the lane, the lane. The lane is where the dogs run. The lane is where the lights blink. The lane is where the people go. I do not go there. I wait in the hollow. I hear the mice. I hear the voles. I hear the shrew. I hear the barn owl

Grassy place. That is the place where the heath is, and the heath is where I hunt. I do not know the name of the heath, but I know it well. It is where the voles run, and the mice hide, and the shrews scuttle. I sit on the branch of the old oak and wait. The heath is my hunting ground, and I know it as well as I know my own name.

Voles. I hear them in the undergrowth, and I see them in the moonlight. They are small and quick, but I am quick too. I strike from the branch, and they are mine. The rest of the night is waiting, and then the hunt again. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A vole. Fat, soft, and slow. I can hear them in the heath, under the leaves, in the clay. They are the easiest to catch. I wait, I listen, and then I strike. The others are too quick, too small, too many. But voles... they are mine. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. I hunt in the long grass with my eyes and ears. I sit still, listen for the rustle of a mouse in the dry leaves. When I hear it, I fly low and strike. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but mice are the best. They are quick, but I am faster. I can hear them under the leaves, even when they are hiding. I eat them whole, bones and all. The long grass is my hunting ground. I know every patch

I swallow whole what I catch. A vole, a mouse, a shrew. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole. It's how I eat. I don't have teeth to chew, so I swallow them whole. I can feel them in my throat, and then they go down. I don't like to think about it. I just do it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A vole. I catch voles in the heath, in the field, in the stream bank. They are small, brown, and quick. I sit still, wait, and then strike. They are the most common, and the most satisfying. I eat them whole, but I do not swallow the bones. I leave them in the stream.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, with a narrow entrance. I line it with dry leaves and feathers. I roost there all night, and the stream is just a few paces away. I can hear the water all the time.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, high in the hollow of the wood. I have been there all my life, and I have raised my young there. The wood is my world, and the hollow is my place. I sit in it and listen for the night, and I call to my mate. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak, the one I have used for twenty years. The bark is thick and the leaves are soft. I sit in the middle of it, and the wind comes through the branches. I can hear the stream from there, and the heath beyond. I have a mate, and we call to each other at dusk. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I have been here for years, and it is safe. The oak is tall and strong, and the hollow is deep. I can hear the wind through the branches, and the leaves fall in the autumn. I have a mate, and we have raised our young here. I am Hoot. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The hollow is in the old oak by the stream. It is wide and deep, with a narrow entrance. I sit in the middle, and the wind comes through the branches. The wood is dry and warm, and the smell of it is old and safe. I have been here for many years. The hollow is my home, and I do not leave it unless I must. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
